questions.stem: A wholesale distributor wants Claude to draft answers to dealer pricing questions. In interviews, the sales-desk manager describes the process as 'read the question, look up the price list, reply.' Yet the desk's own staff take about 20 minutes per question, which seems long for that process. With two weeks left in discovery, which step will MOST reliably reveal the requirements the interviews are missing?

options.text: Send a written survey to every sales-desk employee asking them to list the steps they follow, then merge the answers into a single process map.
Sit with several desk staff while they handle live questions, noting which systems and people they turn to, and keep the real cases you observe.
Build a quick prototype from the manager's description, put it in front of the desk staff, and collect their feedback on what the drafts get wrong.
Hold a second, longer interview with the manager and ask detailed follow-up questions about each of the three steps, including any tools or people involved.

questions.explanation: When the described process and the observed effort don't match, there are hidden steps: a second system checked, a colleague consulted, an approval sought. Watching the work as it happens (shadowing) is the most reliable way to find them. Each hidden step becomes a tool, a data source or an escalation path in the design. The cases you observe also seed a realistic eval set that mirrors the real distribution of work, which is what Anthropic's eval guidance asks for.

whyWrong.A: A survey asks people to describe their own routine from memory. That is exactly how tacit steps get left out, so you would merge several incomplete accounts.
whyWrong.C: A prototype built on a process you already suspect is incomplete spends build time to uncover what an hour of observation would show. Feedback will also focus on draft wording, not missing steps.
whyWrong.D: The manager is the source of the simplified account. More detail from the same person doesn't surface steps that only the people doing the work know about.

questions.mindset: When the story and the effort don't match, watch the work. Hidden steps become tools and escalation paths.

questions.stem: A utility company's customer-service director sets the goal for a Claude-assisted reply tool: 'cut agent handling time on billing disputes substantially.' During discovery you learn that handling time isn't tracked per case type today, and nobody knows how often agents' current replies have to be corrected. The success criteria must be signed off before design begins. What should the architect do FIRST?

options.text: Adopt a widely cited industry figure for AI-assisted handling-time reduction as the target, so the project has an ambitious, externally credible number.
Agree a target of 'at least 40% faster' now, and measure handling time only once the pilot is live, so the team isn't delayed.
Ask Claude to estimate typical handling time from a sample of past dispute transcripts and use its estimate as the baseline for the target.
Measure current handling time and correction rate for billing disputes on a recent sample, then set targets against that baseline with the director.

questions.explanation: A success criterion has to be measurable and achievable, and a target like 'substantially faster' or '40% faster' means nothing without a starting point. Measuring today's handling time and correction rate for this case type gives that baseline. It also adds a quality dimension, so speed can't be bought by sending worse replies. Then the director can set targets with real numbers, and the same measurement becomes the pilot's comparison point.

whyWrong.A: Industry figures can help judge whether a target is achievable, but they are a percentage change on someone else's baseline and case mix. Without this team's own baseline, the result still can't be measured.
whyWrong.B: A target agreed before any baseline exists can't be checked when the pilot ends, because there is nothing to compare against. It also ignores quality.
whyWrong.C: A model's guess about elapsed time from transcripts is not a measurement. Transcripts don't record the time agents spend researching around them.

questions.mindset: No baseline, no target. Measure today before you promise 'better'.

questions.stem: You are running discovery for an internal assistant that will answer managers' questions using employee records pulled from the company's HR system. So far you have interviewed the HR director (the sponsor) and the IT infrastructure lead, and the budget is already approved. The sponsor wants to skip further interviews and start design. Which TWO stakeholders are MOST important to bring in now, because leaving them out is most likely to block go-live late in the project? Choose TWO.

options.text: The owner of the HR system, who controls API access, the field definitions, and how current and complete the employee records are.
A wider group of HR generalists, who can rank the assistant's planned features by usefulness before any design is drafted.
The privacy or data-protection lead, who must approve personal employee data flowing to the model and decide who may see which answers.
The finance team, who can confirm the token budget and decide whether the project should use a smaller model tier to save money.
An internal AI enthusiast group, who can benchmark several candidate models on sample HR questions and recommend which one to choose.

questions.explanation: Late blockers come from stakeholders with veto power over data. The HR system owner controls whether the assistant can read the records at all, under what permissions, and how good the data is. The privacy or data-protection lead has to approve personal data going to a model, and decide who may see which answers. Anthropic documents how API data is handled and retained, and those facts need to go in front of that lead early. Either of these people can stop a finished build.

whyWrong.B: Ranking features helps, but more HR users won't block go-live. They refine scope; they don't hold a veto over access or data handling.
whyWrong.D: The stem says the budget is approved. Choosing a model tier is a design trade-off settled with evals, not a missing approval.
whyWrong.E: Comparing models is design work for later, decided against agreed success criteria. A model choice doesn't remove a data-access or privacy blocker.

questions.mindset: Find everyone who can say no, especially data owners and privacy, before you design.

questions.stem: Discovery for a telecom's customer-chat assistant began with one goal: answer plan and billing questions. In each workshop the sponsor adds capabilities, most recently issuing account credits, changing customers' plans and updating addresses. The launch date hasn't moved, and none of the new capabilities has an owner or an acceptance test. What is the MOST effective way for the architect to handle this in discovery?

options.text: Rank each capability as must-have or later, write explicit non-goals for version 1 (such as 'no account changes'), and get sponsor sign-off on the scoped brief.
Accept every capability into version 1, but build the assistant as a general agent with broad account tools so new requests can be added without redesign.
Keep every capability in scope and tell the sponsor the launch date is at risk, leaving the delivery team to decide what to drop near launch.
Accept the capabilities in the requirements, but write a system prompt telling Claude to perform account changes only when the customer clearly requests one.

questions.explanation: Scope creep in discovery is handled with priorities and stated non-goals agreed by the sponsor. A non-goal such as 'version 1 makes no account changes' is a real requirement. It also shrinks the tool surface, which is least privilege in practice. Anthropic's guidance is to start with the simplest system that meets the need and add capability only when it clearly pays off. The deferred items go on a backlog, each with an owner and an acceptance test.

whyWrong.B: Broad account tools grant write access nobody has specified or tested. 'Easy to extend' is no reason to take on that risk in version 1.
whyWrong.C: Pointing out the risk without making a scope decision leaves the cut to whoever is under pressure near launch. That is the worst point to make it.
whyWrong.D: A prompt instruction is not a scope decision or a control. Account-changing actions still need owners, acceptance tests and, often, deterministic checks.

questions.mindset: Non-goals are requirements. Write them down and get them signed.

questions.stem: A retailer wants Claude to turn the product reviews it receives each week into a digest for category managers. Discovery has already settled what the digest must contain and how its quality will be judged. The architect has one more session with the business team before the design review and wants to spend it on the findings that will MOST change the architecture that gets proposed. Which TWO questions should the architect ask? Choose TWO.

options.text: Which AI vendors the category team has already seen demos from, so the proposal can be positioned against those alternatives in the review.
Whether the digest must be ready within minutes of the week closing, or whether an overnight run before managers start work is acceptable.
Whether the category managers would prefer the digest as bullet points or as short paragraphs, so the output format is fixed before design.
How many reviews arrive per week, in which languages, and whether volume peaks are predictable, for example around promotions, holidays and seasonal sales.
Which model tier the sponsor expects the team to use, so the design can be built around that choice rather than revisited later.

questions.explanation: Functional requirements are agreed, so the remaining discovery time should go on the non-functional constraints that shape the architecture. Whether results are needed in near real time or can be produced overnight decides whether the work can run asynchronously; Anthropic's Message Batches API is designed for large volumes that don't need immediate responses and processes them at a lower cost. Volume, language mix and peak behaviour decide throughput, rate-limit planning, cost and whether multilingual handling is a requirement. Both answers change the design; the others don't.

whyWrong.A: Competitive positioning may matter to the sales conversation, but it doesn't change how the system should be built.
whyWrong.C: Output formatting is a prompt-level detail that can change in a day. It doesn't affect processing mode, cost or scale.
whyWrong.E: Model tier is an output of design, chosen by testing candidates against the agreed quality criteria. Asking the sponsor to pick it in discovery fixes a decision before the evidence exists.

questions.mindset: Once 'what' is agreed, ask about 'how fast', 'how much' and 'how often'. Those answers shape the architecture.

questions.stem: An accounts-payable team wants Claude to flag invoices that look like duplicates or overbilling before payment. In discovery, the controller says only 'it should catch the bad ones.' A flagged invoice is held for a clerk to review, which delays a supplier payment. A missed duplicate is usually paid and is hard to recover. The architect has to define requirements that will drive how flagging and review are designed. Which discovery step is MOST important?

options.text: Agree that the system should maximize the share of bad invoices it catches, because a missed duplicate costs more than any delay a hold causes a supplier.
Agree that Claude will attach a confidence score to each flag, and that the controller will pick a cutoff once the pilot shows real scores.
Set one target for overall accuracy on a labeled sample of past invoices, since that figure covers both kinds of error the controller cares about.
Quantify with the controller the cost of a missed duplicate and of a needless hold, plus clerk review capacity, and set separate targets per error type.

questions.explanation: The two errors cost very different amounts, and someone has to absorb the false alarms. The design choice of how aggressively to flag and how much to route to clerks depends on what each error costs and how many reviews the clerks can actually do. Anthropic's eval guidance favors specific, multidimensional criteria over one blended number, and its example criteria separate minor errors from serious ones. Separate targets (for example, a minimum share of duplicates caught and a maximum hold volume per day) can be tested and defended.

whyWrong.A: Catching everything with no limit on false alarms can swamp the clerks and delay many legitimate payments. The cost of holds is part of the requirement.
whyWrong.B: A model's self-reported confidence is not a calibrated probability. Leaving the cutoff until after the pilot means there was no agreed requirement to design against.
whyWrong.C: A single accuracy figure hides the trade-off. Duplicates are rare, so a system that flags almost nothing can still score high accuracy.

questions.mindset: When errors cost different amounts, set a target for each error type, not one accuracy number.

questions.stem: A parcel carrier asked for 'a Claude agent for all inbound customer emails.' Discovery data shows that about three-quarters of the emails ask only for a delivery status, which an existing tracking API already returns from the tracking number. The rest are free-text complaints, claims and unusual requests. The sponsor still describes the project as 'the AI agent.' What is the BEST requirement to bring out of discovery?

options.text: Route every email through a single autonomous agent that holds the tracking API as a tool, so all emails are handled consistently by one system.
Handle tracking-number status requests with a deterministic lookup and template, and use Claude only for the free-text remainder, with defined escalation rules.
Defer the status-request group to a later phase and scope version 1 to complaints and claims only, where AI adds the most value.
Have Claude classify and answer every email, including status requests, so the sponsor gets the full 'AI agent' experience they asked for.

questions.explanation: Discovery should find the simplest solution that meets the need. Anthropic's agent guidance says that may mean not using an LLM, or an agent, for part of the work. A status lookup keyed on a tracking number is deterministic, cheap and exact. Claude adds value where language is unstructured and judgment is needed. Writing that split into the requirements cuts cost and risk while still meeting the sponsor's goal.

whyWrong.A: One autonomous agent for everything adds cost, latency and unpredictability to a large, simple group of requests that code already handles exactly.
whyWrong.C: Deferring the status requests leaves three-quarters of the emails unhandled when a lookup-and-template path needs no AI work at all. The requirement should name that deterministic path, not postpone it.
whyWrong.D: This designs to the label the sponsor used, not to the requirement. An LLM call per status request costs more and adds variance with no benefit.

questions.mindset: Use AI where judgment is needed and plain code where the answer is a lookup.

questions.stem: A bank wants a Claude assistant that answers branch staff's procedure questions from its internal policy library. In discovery you find that the library holds several versions of some procedures with no 'current' marker. Some documents have no named owner, and retired procedures were never removed. The sponsor sees this as an implementation detail the engineers can work around. What should the architect record as the discovery outcome?

options.text: Plan to load the entire library into a large context window so Claude can compare the conflicting versions and work out which procedure is current.
Plan to add a system-prompt instruction telling Claude to prefer the most recently dated document whenever two versions of a procedure conflict.
Record as requirements a named owner for each source, a current-version and retirement process, and a check that the content is clean before launch.
Plan to fine-tune a model on the whole policy library so the right procedures are learned directly and the document conflicts stop mattering.

questions.explanation: A retrieval-grounded assistant can only be as correct as the content it retrieves. Retrieval brings back whatever relevant chunks exist, including outdated ones, and citations will then faithfully point staff to a retired procedure. Content ownership, version status and retirement belong in the requirements, with named owners, because they decide answer quality and keep deciding it after launch. Treating them as an engineering workaround hides a business-process gap.

whyWrong.A: Putting conflicting documents in context leaves the model to guess which is current. Nothing in a long context can tell it which version the bank actually enforces.
whyWrong.B: Recency is not authority. A newer draft or local variant can be more recent than the approved procedure, and no prompt can tell them apart without metadata.
whyWrong.D: Fine-tuning on conflicting, unowned content builds the conflicts into the model. Updates also become harder, and answers can't cite a current source.

questions.mindset: Grounded answers are only as good as the sources. Content ownership is a requirement, not a workaround.

questions.stem: A travel company wants a customer-facing trip-planning assistant. In discovery, the product owner has described the happy path in detail: the customer asks, the assistant suggests itineraries and answers follow-up questions. Nobody has yet described what should happen when the assistant can't or shouldn't answer, such as a medical question about a destination, a complaint about a cancelled trip, or a refund request. The requirements brief is due in a week. Which TWO discovery findings are MOST important to capture so that the design has a workable fallback? Choose TWO.

options.text: A sponsor's estimate of how rarely such requests come up, so the fallback can be designed later if the pilot shows it is actually needed.
A system-prompt instruction telling the assistant to be careful with sensitive topics, drafted now so engineering can start building without waiting for the brief.
Who handles those cases today, through which channel, and how quickly they must respond, so the assistant has a real hand-off target with an owner.
The model's refusal rate on a public safety benchmark, to estimate how often the fallback will be triggered once the assistant is live.
The topics the assistant must not handle itself, agreed with legal and customer service, with a concrete example of each to seed the eval set.

questions.explanation: An assistant that is allowed to say it can't help, and to hand off, is safer than one forced to answer everything; Anthropic's hallucination guidance explicitly recommends giving Claude permission to decline, and its agent guidance says to pause for humans at checkpoints. But a hand-off only works if discovery has found the real destination: who takes over, through what channel, and how fast. The out-of-scope topics also have to be agreed with the people accountable for them (legal, customer service), and a worked example of each turns the boundary into an eval case rather than a vague instruction.

whyWrong.A: Low frequency doesn't mean low impact. A single mishandled refund or medical question can do more damage than many good itineraries, and designing the fallback later means launching without one.
whyWrong.B: A prompt instruction is a design artefact, not a requirement, and 'be careful' is untestable. Without agreed topics and a hand-off target there is nothing for the instruction to point to.
whyWrong.D: A public benchmark measures refusals on someone else's prompts. It says nothing about this company's customers, topics or escalation path.

questions.mindset: Design the unhappy path in discovery: what the assistant must not handle, who takes over, and how fast.

questions.stem: After two weeks of interviews for a claims-intake assistant, the architect has drafted a requirements brief. Operations, the claims-quality team and compliance each used words like 'urgent claim' and 'complete submission' in their interviews, and nobody has checked that they mean the same thing. Design starts next week. What is the MOST effective way to confirm the requirements before design?

options.text: Hold a joint walkthrough of real sample claims and expected outcomes ('given this claim, the assistant does X'), resolving every disagreement before sign-off.
Email the full brief to all three groups with a one-week deadline, and treat silence as approval so design can start on schedule.
Have Claude summarize the interview transcripts into a single definitions glossary and attach it to the brief as the agreed meaning of each term.
Start design on schedule and settle any differences in meaning during user acceptance testing, when the groups can react to the working system.

questions.explanation: Hidden disagreements over terms like 'urgent' or 'complete' only come out when each group applies them to the same concrete cases. Walking through real examples with expected outcomes forces those definitions into the open. Each worked example then becomes an eval case, which turns the brief into the specific, testable criteria that Anthropic says to settle before prompt work begins.

whyWrong.B: Silence is not agreement. Each group will read its own meaning into the same words, and the conflict will surface during the build.
whyWrong.C: A glossary distilled from transcripts can blend conflicting meanings into smooth wording. No stakeholder has agreed to it.
whyWrong.D: Discovering a definition conflict at UAT means reworking prompts, routing rules and evals at the most expensive point in the project.

questions.mindset: Confirm requirements with concrete examples. Shared words hide different meanings.

questions.stem: An engineering firm's CIO must approve the architecture for an assistant that answers questions from a design-standards library that the standards team updates monthly. The architect has proposed retrieval over the library with answers that cite the clause they rely on. The CIO asks: 'Why not just train Claude on our standards so it knows them? That sounds simpler than all this retrieval machinery.' Which reply is BOTH accurate and appropriate for the CIO?

options.text: Training a model is a research-grade technique the firm's team lacks, and retrieval is what most vendors do today, so it is the safer default even if the answers would end up much the same.

Knowledge trained into a model is frozen until it is retrained, so monthly updates would leave it answering from stale standards. Retrieval reads the current library and cites the clause, so the standards team keeps control.

Retrieval is more accurate in every case because the model sees the exact text of the standard, so once the pipeline is built there is no need for a separate evaluation of answer quality before the assistant launches.

Both approaches would give similar answers, but retrieval lets engineering reuse the vector database the firm already licenses, which keeps the project inside this year's approved budget and avoids starting a new procurement cycle.

questions.explanation: The CIO's question is a real one, so it deserves the real reason in business terms: the standards change monthly, and the firm needs the assistant to reflect the current version and show its source. Anthropic's guidance for knowledge-base questions is to ground the model in the documents at request time (in the prompt for small corpora, through retrieval for larger ones) and to have Claude cite the passages it relied on. Knowledge trained into model weights can't be updated by editing a document or audited by clause. The reply explains freshness, traceability and ownership without jargon and without overclaiming.

whyWrong.A: Appealing to skills gaps and vendor habit dodges the question. It gives the CIO no business reason, and 'results are similar' concedes a point that isn't true for monthly-changing content.
whyWrong.C: Seeing the exact text doesn't make retrieval right 'in every case'; retrieval can miss the relevant passage. Claiming no evaluation is needed is both inaccurate and a governance red flag.
whyWrong.D: Licence reuse is a procurement convenience, not the architectural reason. It also wrongly concedes that the two approaches would answer equally well as the standards change.

questions.mindset: Answer 'why not just train it?' with freshness, traceability and ownership, not with jargon or convenience.

questions.stem: A logistics company's Claude agent reads inbound supplier emails and can look up orders and draft replies. Changing a delivery address needs a human click to approve. At the design review, the CISO asks: 'Is prompt injection solved in this design? Yes or no.' The team's controls are a system prompt that tells Claude to ignore instructions found in emails, read-only lookup tools, and the human approval step. Which answer is MOST appropriate?

options.text: No. Injection can be reduced but not eliminated; show how read-only tools and the approval step limit the damage, and name the remaining risk and how it is monitored.
Yes. The system prompt explicitly tells Claude to treat instructions found in emails as untrusted data, so injected instructions will not be acted on and no further controls are needed.
Yes, for practical purposes. Current Claude models are trained to be skeptical of instructions in tool results, so the remaining risk is too small to justify extra controls or monitoring.
No. Recommend pausing the project until a vendor can certify that prompt injection is fully prevented, so the CISO is never asked to accept a risk that cannot be measured.

questions.explanation: An honest trade-off answer separates what is guaranteed from what is only less likely. Prompt-level defenses and model training reduce injection but don't eliminate it. Anthropic's guidance on safe agents and its guardrail docs recommend layered controls. Here, read-only tools and a human approval step on the one sensitive write limit the damage if an injection succeeds. The CISO can sign off on a named residual risk with monitoring; a false 'yes' would fall apart at the first incident.

whyWrong.B: A prompt instruction is a probabilistic defense, not a control. Presenting it as a guarantee misrepresents the risk to the person who has to accept it.
whyWrong.C: Model training does make Claude more skeptical of instructions in tool results, but Anthropic's own guidance treats that as one layer and still recommends least privilege, screening and monitoring. 'Too small to need controls' contradicts it.
whyWrong.D: No credible vendor certifies complete prevention. Waiting for one blocks the project without improving the design, which already limits impact.

questions.mindset: Don't promise what a prompt can't guarantee. Show how the architecture limits the impact, and name what's left.

questions.stem: An architect must explain one decision to two audiences in the same week: send routine support tickets to a smaller, faster Claude model and escalate complex ones to a larger model. The executive committee will approve the budget and the risk; the engineering leads will implement the routing. Which TWO practices BEST serve both audiences? Choose TWO.

options.text: Present the same detailed technical deck to both groups, so everyone sees identical information and nobody can later claim something was left out.
Open the executive session with a public benchmark leaderboard showing how the two model tiers rank on general tasks, since that is the most objective evidence.
Give executives a one-page summary of cost per ticket, eval-set quality and the risk, with routing logic and eval detail in an engineering appendix.
State the remaining downside plainly (for example, some complex tickets may be routed to the smaller model first) and name who has accepted that risk.
Leave the routing errors out of the executive version so the committee is not distracted, and cover them only in the engineering session.

questions.explanation: The same decision needs different framing: executives need cost per outcome, measured quality on the team's own eval set and the risk, while engineers need routing rules and eval detail. Both versions must be honest about the downside and who owns it. Anthropic's model-selection guidance frames the tier choice as balancing capability, speed and cost against the task, and its eval guidance stresses measuring on your own task, not generic leaderboards.

whyWrong.A: Identical detail for both groups buries executives in mechanics and leaves the decision they actually own unclear.
whyWrong.B: A public leaderboard doesn't measure this team's tickets. Executives need cost and quality on their own workload.
whyWrong.E: Hiding the known downside from the people approving the risk turns sign-off into a misinformed approval.

questions.mindset: Same decision, different framing for each audience. The risk is always disclosed and always owned.

questions.stem: For a high-volume document-classification service, the architect proposes a smaller Claude model. On the agreed 1,000-document eval set it meets the accuracy target, and its latency and per-document cost are well below the larger model's. A senior VP pushes back: 'This is customer-facing. Use the biggest model; I don't want to cut corners.' What is the MOST effective response?

options.text: Switch to the largest model to keep the VP's support, and plan to revisit the choice after launch if the monthly bill becomes a problem.
Explain that smaller models are now nearly as capable as larger ones, so the VP's concern about quality is outdated and can be safely dismissed.
Propose running both models in production on all live traffic indefinitely, and showing whichever output looks better to each customer who submits a document.
Show both models' results against the target with cost and latency per document, and offer escalation to the larger model for low-confidence cases.

questions.explanation: The VP's real concern is quality risk, so answer it with evidence against the success criterion everyone agreed. Anthropic's model-selection and latency guidance frames model choice as a balance of capability, speed and cost for the specific task. Showing that the smaller model meets the bar, and pricing what the larger one would add, makes the trade-off concrete. Offering escalation for hard cases speaks directly to the 'don't cut corners' worry without paying top price for every document.

whyWrong.A: This gives up an evidence-based decision to avoid friction, and pushes the cost problem to after launch when it is harder to change.
whyWrong.B: Dismissing the concern with a generalization is neither evidence nor persuasive. The case should rest on this task's measured results.
whyWrong.C: Running both models on all traffic doubles cost and adds complexity, and 'whichever looks better' is not a defined selection rule.

questions.mindset: Answer 'use the biggest model' with eval results, cost per task and a fallback for the hard cases.

questions.stem: A lending firm's assistant drafts adverse-action letters, and a compliance analyst reviews each one before it is sent. To hit a launch date, the business owner wants to drop the review step. The eval shows that 4% of drafts contain a wrong or missing reason for denial, mostly on applications with several reasons. The architect thinks removing review is too risky but does not own the decision. What should the architect do?

options.text: Keep the review step running quietly after launch, without telling the business owner, so the risk stays controlled whatever the owner decides.
Explain the 4% error rate as business and regulatory exposure, propose review only for multi-reason applications, and record the decision with a named owner.
Refuse to approve launch until the error rate is zero, because any defect in an adverse-action letter is unacceptable in a regulated process.
Remove the review step as requested, and add a stronger system-prompt instruction telling Claude to list every denial reason accurately and double-check multi-reason applications.

questions.explanation: When a stakeholder wants to accept a risk the architect disagrees with, the architect's job is to make the risk clear in business terms, offer a less risky alternative, and make sure the decision and its owner are recorded. Keeping review only where the eval shows errors cluster cuts most of the delay while keeping humans where Anthropic's agent guidance says checkpoints matter most. The written decision makes it auditable.

whyWrong.A: A hidden control undermines governance and trust. The business owner would be deciding on false information about how the system runs.
whyWrong.C: A zero-error demand isn't achievable for a probabilistic system and ignores the targeted partial-review option. It also oversteps a decision the architect doesn't own.
whyWrong.D: A prompt change is not shown to fix the error cluster, and it can't replace a control in a regulated step. Complying silently also hides the risk.

questions.mindset: You may not own the decision, but you own making the risk visible, offering an alternative and recording who accepted it.

questions.stem: A year ago a decision record approved putting a company's whole policy handbook into every prompt, with prompt caching, for an employee Q&A assistant. Product, finance and security signed it. The record says to revisit if the handbook grows enough that cost or response time drift past agreed limits. The handbook has since grown several-fold and both limits are now exceeded. The engineers want to move to retrieval. How should the architect handle the change?

options.text: Let the engineers switch to retrieval as an internal implementation detail, since users will still see the same assistant and stakeholders don't need to be involved.
Keep the current design because the original stakeholders signed off on it, and ask finance to raise the cost limit to match the larger handbook.
Reopen the decision with current cost, latency and eval data, get sign-off from the same groups, and supersede the old record with a new one.
Ask Claude to compress the handbook into a shorter summary for the prompt, so the original approved design can stay in place without new approvals.

questions.explanation: A revisit trigger exists so a decision is reopened through the same channel it was made in once circumstances change. Moving from whole handbook in context to retrieval changes cost, freshness, failure modes (missed retrievals) and possibly data flows. Product, finance and security should see current numbers and approve again. A new record that supersedes the old one keeps the history traceable. Anthropic's retrieval guidance describes exactly this threshold: whole-corpus prompting suits small knowledge bases, and retrieval scales beyond them.

whyWrong.A: Retrieval changes how the system can fail and what it costs. Swapping it in silently bypasses the people who signed the original decision.
whyWrong.B: Sign-off was conditional on revisit triggers that have now fired. Raising the limit to fit the design reverses the logic of the decision record.
whyWrong.D: A lossy summary changes answer quality without evidence or approval. It's a workaround, not a decision.

questions.mindset: When a revisit trigger fires, reopen the decision openly with fresh data and the same sign-off group.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company's medical-information assistant is designed to say it can't answer when the approved documents don't support an answer, and to route those questions to a specialist. In the pilot, the commercial director counts the 'I can't answer that' replies as failures and asks the architect to 'make it always give an answer.' The eval shows 85% correct answers, 12% declined and 3% wrong. What is the BEST way to communicate the trade-off?

options.text: Agree to remove the option to decline, because the director owns the commercial goal and a complete answer to every question is what the field teams and their customers expect.
Explain that the 12% decline rate is a temporary limitation of the current model, and that moving to a larger model will let the assistant answer every question correctly.
Show that allowing declines keeps the wrong-answer rate low, that forcing answers turns declines into wrong answers, and offer to cut declines by filling gaps in the approved documents.
Report the declines as successes in the pilot metrics, since a referral to a specialist is a safe outcome, so the headline rate improves while the design stays unchanged.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's hallucination guidance recommends explicitly letting Claude say it doesn't know when the sources don't support an answer. Declining is a safety feature, not a defect. The director needs the trade-off in outcome terms: answers forced on unsupported questions become wrong medical information instead of specialist referrals. The architect should present the correct, declined and wrong split, and offer real levers that reduce declines safely, such as filling content gaps.

whyWrong.A: Removing the option to decline in a medical-information setting trades visible referrals for invisible wrong answers. That risk must be shown, not just accepted.
whyWrong.B: A larger model cannot answer correctly from documents that don't contain the answer, and promising 100% correct is not credible.
whyWrong.D: A referral may be a safe outcome, but relabeling declines as successes without agreement misreports the results and destroys trust in the metrics everyone uses to decide.

questions.mindset: 'I don't know' is a design choice. Show what forcing an answer would cost.
